name: Drug Repurposing
title: Drug Repurposing
answer: Drug repurposing is the practice of finding new therapeutic uses for medicines that are already approved or have passed early safety testing. It sits within drug discovery and molecular simulation because the work often begins with computational screening rather than a new chemical synthesis. The goal is to shorten development timelines and lower costs by reusing existing safety, dosing, and manufacturing knowledge. This page covers methods that match existing drugs to new disease targets, new patient subgroups, or new combinations.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drug repurposing is the practice of finding new therapeutic uses for medicines that are already approved or have passed early safety testing. It sits within drug discovery and molecular simulation because the work often begins with computational screening rather than a new chemical synthesis. The goal is to shorten development timelines and lower costs by reusing existing safety, dosing, and manufacturing knowledge. This page covers methods that match existing drugs to new disease targets, new patient subgroups, or new combinations.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on high performance computing clusters, cloud GPU and TPU instances, and large curated databases of drug structures, protein targets, gene expression profiles, and electronic health records. Common infrastructure includes molecular docking engines, graph databases for drug target disease networks, and model registries for reproducible screening. Many groups use containerized pipelines that move from data cleaning to candidate ranking in a single workflow. Storage and compute are often separated so that large chemical libraries can be screened without moving raw data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical workflow starts by defining a disease signature or a protein target, then screening a library of existing drugs against that signature. Molecular docking simulates how a drug fits a binding site, while transcriptomic matching compares gene expression changes caused by a drug to changes seen in disease. Knowledge graph models score paths between a drug, a target, and a disease using known relationships from literature and databases. The strongest computational hits are then tested in cell or animal models before any human study is considered.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Data provenance is a central concern because repurposing draws on clinical trial records, spontaneous adverse event reports, genomic biobanks, and published literature, each with different quality and consent terms. A model trained on biased or incomplete data can produce plausible but false repurposing leads, so results need independent replication. Intellectual property questions arise when a new use is found for an off patent drug, and regulatory pathways such as the 505(b)(2) route in the United States require careful documentation of prior evidence. The site tracks 210 compliance and regulation pages, some of which address evidentiary standards for AI generated hypotheses.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Repurposing is moving toward multimodal models that combine chemical structure, electronic health records, and real world evidence in a single ranking system. Federated learning across hospital networks may allow new safety and efficacy signals to be found without moving patient data. Foundation models pretrained on molecular and clinical text are likely to reduce the need for bespoke training sets. The field is also shifting from single drug single target predictions to combination and patient subgroup repurposing, where the same drug may be matched to a narrow responder population.
